# Abnormal labor and delivery

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Labor, delivery, and associated disorders > Abnormal labor and delivery*

[Original Article Link](/library/Xl09vT)

---

## Summary

Abnormal <u>labor</u> and delivery occurs as a result of complications before and/or during <u>birth</u>. <u>Prolonged stages of labor</u> can lead to <u>active-phase labor arrest</u>, <u>fetal malpresentation</u> may cause <u>mechanical obstruction of labor</u>, <u>abnormal rupture of membranes</u> can increase the risk of <u>chorioamnionitis</u> and <u>neonatal sepsis</u>, and <u>umbilical cord complications</u> can increase the risk of <u>birth asphyxia</u> and <u>stillbirth</u>. Management of abnormal <u>labor</u> and delivery is typically tailored to the patient and can include <u>induction of labor</u>, <u>prophylaxis for neonatal GBS infection</u>, <u>assisted vaginal delivery</u>, special obstetrical maneuvers, <u>intrauterine resuscitation</u>, and/or emergency <u>cesarean delivery</u>.




See also “<u>Normal labor and delivery</u>,” “<u>Preterm labor</u>,” “<u>Postpartum hemorrhage</u>,” “<u>Chorioamnionitis</u>,” “<u>Neonatal resuscitation</u>,” and “<u>Birth traumas</u>.”

---

## Abnormalities in fetal orientation

<u>Fetal malpresentation</u> and <u>fetal malposition</u> are associated with increased <u>perinatal</u> risks and may require assisted delivery or <u>cesarean delivery</u> to prevent maternal and fetal complications (see “<u>Obstructed labor</u>”).




### Fetal malpresentation




* Definition: any <u>fetal presentation</u> or fetal lie that is not the <u>cephalic presentation</u>

* Examples

* <u>Breech presentations</u> 

* <u>Frank breech</u>

* <u>Complete breech</u>

* <u>Single footling breech</u>

* <u>Double footling breech</u>

* <u>Compound presentation</u>

* <u>Shoulder presentation</u>

* <u>Transverse lie</u>

* <u>Oblique lie</u>

### Fetal malposition




* Definition: a <u>fetal position</u> in which the fetus is in the <u>cephalic presentation</u> but not oriented anteriorly

* Examples

* <u>Occiput posterior position</u>

* <u>Occiput transverse position</u>

## Abnormal stages of labor

### Definitions




* Prolonged (protracted) labor: abnormally slow progression of the <u>labor</u> process, typically marked by delayed <u>cervical dilatation</u> in the first stage or delayed descent or expulsive phase in the second stage (see "<u>Overview of abnormal stages of labor</u>")  [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)[[2]](/library/wbVhDG0)

* Labor arrest: a complete halting of <u>labor</u> progression despite adequate <u>augmentation of labor</u> [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)





### <u>Risk factors</u> for prolonged or <u>arrested labor</u>




* First and second <u>stages of labor</u> [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)

* <u>Induction of labor</u> (latent phase only)

* <u>Nulliparity</u>

* Maternal <u>obesity</u>

* <u>Advanced maternal age</u>

* Abnormalities of the 3 Ps of labor

* <u>Pelvis</u>: size and shape of the maternal <u>pelvis</u> (e.g., small bony <u>pelvis</u>)

* Passenger: size and position of the <u>infant</u> (e.g., <u>fetal macrosomia</u> or abnormal orientation)

* Power: strength and frequency of contractions (e.g., dysfunctional contractions )

* Cephalopelvic disproportion: The fetal head size is disproportionately large for the maternal <u>pelvis</u>.

* Second stage only

* <u>Epidural anesthesia</u>

* Delayed pushing [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)[[3]](/library/1ZV20G0)

* Third stage of <u>labor</u> [[4]](/library/Y-dnDs0)

* Inadequate contractions

* Abnormal <u>placental</u> implantation

* Distortions of the <u>uterine cavity</u> (e.g., <u>fibroids</u>)





### Types of <u>abnormal labor stages</u>




| <br>Overview of abnormal stages of labor [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stage |  | <br>Definition <br> | Duration |  |
| <u>Nulliparous</u> patients | <u>Multiparous</u> patients |  |  |  |
| Prolonged first stage of labor | Prolonged latent phase of labor | <br>* Slow progression (contraction frequency) with a <u>cervical dilation</u> ≤ 6 cm<br><br> | <br>* > 20 hours<br><br> | <br>* > 14 hours<br><br> |
| Prolonged active phase of labor | <br>* ≥ 6 cm <u>cervical dilation</u> with delayed further dilation (< 1 cm per 2 hours)<br><br> |  |  |  |
| Arrested active phase |  | <br>* ≥ 6 cm <u>cervical dilation</u> with ruptured membranes and no cervical change after one of the following:<br><br>* ≥ 4 hours of adequate contractions (≥ 200 <u>Montevideo units</u>)<br><br>* > 6 hours of inadequate contractions with <u>augmentation of labor</u><br><br> |  |  |
| Prolonged second stage of labor |  | <br>* Prolonged expulsive phase from complete <u>cervical dilation</u> (> 10 cm) and effacement (100%) to delivery.<br><br> | <br>* > 3 hours (> 4 hours in patients who received an epidural)<br><br> | <br>* > 2 hours (> 3 hours in patients who received an epidural)<br><br> |
| Arrested <u>second stage of labor</u> |  | <br>* Arrest of fetal descent or rotation despite adequate contractions<br><br> | <br>* Can be diagnosed anytime during the <u>second stage of labor</u><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Prolonged third stage of labor</u> [[4]](/library/Y-dnDs0)<br> |  | <br>* <u>Placenta</u> has not been delivered 30 minutes after <u>birth</u> [[4]](/library/Y-dnDs0)<br><br> |  |  |





### Management of <u>abnormal labor stages</u> [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)




* Tailor management based on stage and whether <u>labor</u> is prolonged or arrested.

* Ensure adequate <u>obstetric analgesia</u> throughout.

* Consider nonpharmacological adjuvant <u>supportive care</u>.  

* Continuous one-on-one support

* Hydration

* Ambulation and upright positioning

* Prepare for potential management failure (e.g., ensure staff are available for <u>cesarean delivery</u>).





#### <u>First stage of labor</u>




* <u>Prolonged first stage of labor</u> [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)

* Start augmentation of labor, the process of stimulating uterine contractions with <u>amniotomy</u> and/or <u>oxytocin</u> infusion.

* Consider inserting an intrauterine catheter to monitor adequacy of contractions and titrate <u>oxytocin</u> as needed.

* <u>Arrested active phase</u>: : <u>cesarean delivery</u> [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)[[5]](/library/CAdqNs0)





> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>expectant management</u> for <u>prolonged latent stage of labor</u> using <u>shared decision-making</u>. [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)




#### <u>Second stage of labor</u>




* Prolonged stage [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)[[5]](/library/CAdqNs0)

* Address <u>modifiable risk factors</u>.

* Hypotonic uterine contractions: Start <u>augmentation of labor</u> or increase the rate of <u>oxytocin</u> infusion if already started.

* Fetal malpositioning: Consider manual rotation.

* For patients without an epidural, encourage upright positioning.  [[5]](/library/CAdqNs0)

* Consider delayed pushing.

* Arrested stage: : <u>assisted vaginal delivery</u> or <u>cesarean delivery</u> [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)





#### <u>Prolonged third stage of labor</u>




* Continue <u>active management of the third stage of labor</u>. [[4]](/library/Y-dnDs0)

* If the <u>placenta</u> is incomplete or an accessory <u>placenta</u> is suspected: [[6]](/library/NOb-sF)

* Manually palpate the <u>uterine cavity</u>.

* Remove remaining tissue with manual extraction or <u>suction curettage</u>. [[4]](/library/Y-dnDs0)

* See "<u>Retained placenta</u>" for details.





### Complications




* Maternal [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)

* Infection (e.g., <u>chorioamnionitis</u>, <u>endometritis</u>) ;  [[4]](/library/Y-dnDs0)

* Need for <u>assisted vaginal delivery</u> or <u>cesarean delivery</u>

* <u>Postpartum hemorrhage</u> [[4]](/library/Y-dnDs0)

* <u>Perineal lacerations</u>

* Neonatal [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)

* <u>Perinatal asphyxia and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Sepsis</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Birth traumas</u>

* <u>Death</u>





### Prevention [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)[[5]](/library/CAdqNs0)




* Avoid admission for low-risk patients during latent <u>labor</u>.  [[5]](/library/CAdqNs0)

* Encourage continuous <u>labor</u> support.

* Prior to <u>induction of labor</u>, use <u>cervical ripening</u> agents if the <u>cervix</u> appears unfavorable.

## Mechanical obstruction of labor

### Definition [[7]](/library/syWtgL0)



* The arrest of vaginal delivery as a result of a mechanical obstruction




### <u>Risk factors</u>




* <u>Fetal macrosomia</u> (may be physiological or pathological, e.g., due to <u>hydrocephalus</u>)

* <u>Fetal malpresentation</u> or malposition

* Uterine abnormalities, e.g., a <u>tumor</u> (e.g., <u>uterine leiomyoma</u>), deformities of the maternal <u>pelvis</u>, <u>bicornuate uterus</u>, <u>multiparity</u>

* <u>Placenta previa</u>

* Short <u>umbilical cord</u>

* <u>Oligohydramnios</u>, <u>polyhydramnios</u>





### Clinical features [[8]](/library/8HWOH50)[[9]](/library/zHWrG50)




#### Maternal




* Exhaustion

* Frequent uterine contractions

* <u>Edematous</u> <u>vulva</u>

* <u>Bandl ring</u>





#### Fetal




* High presenting part that is not engaged with the <u>pelvis</u>

* <u>Rupture of membranes</u>

* Significant <u>head molding</u>

* <u>Caput succedaneum</u>

* <u>Fetal distress</u>





### Prelabor management




Patients with an increased risk for <u>mechanical obstruction of labor</u> should create a <u>birth</u> plan with their <u>obstetrician</u>, possibly including a scheduled <u>cesarean delivery</u>.




* <u>Breech presentation</u> [[10]](/library/aAWQRL0)

* < 37 weeks: no intervention necessary, as most fetuses spontaneously convert to a <u>cephalic presentation</u> as they get closer to term [[11]](/library/IKWY3m0)

* ≥ 37 weeks: Consider <u>external cephalic version</u>.

* A planned <u>cesarean delivery</u> may be necessary if <u>external cephalic version</u> is not performed, unsuccessful, or contraindicated.

* <u>Manually assisted vaginal delivery</u> may be considered for low-risk <u>pregnancies</u> if the patient wants to avoid <u>surgery</u>.

* <u>Transverse lie</u>

* < 37 weeks: no intervention necessary, as the majority of fetuses spontaneously convert to a cephalic or <u>breech presentation</u> before <u>labor</u> [[12]](/library/Gp1BI30)

* ≥ 37 weeks: Consider <u>external cephalic version</u>. [[13]](/library/1uW2JM0)





> [!TIP]
> Primary <u>cesarean delivery</u> may be chosen for patients at high risk of <u>mechanical obstruction of labor</u> (e.g., due to congenital fetal anomalies or maternal <u>risk factors</u>). [[14]](/library/0AWeRL0)




#### External cephalic version [[13]](/library/1uW2JM0)




* Indication: noncephalic fetal lie (e.g., <u>breech presentation</u>, <u>transverse lie</u>) after 37 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Contraindications  [[13]](/library/1uW2JM0)[[15]](/library/W6WPPm0)

* <u>Indications for cesarean delivery</u>

* <u>Placental abruption</u>

* <u>Nonreassuring fetal status</u>

* Active <u>labor</u> or ruptured membranes

* <u>Oligohydramnios</u>

* Procedure: manual adjustment of <u>fetal position</u> by applying pressure on the gravid abdomen to achieve a <u>vertex presentation</u>





### Active <u>labor</u> management [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




#### Approach




* Immediately consult obstetrics, neonatology, and anesthesia if <u>mechanical obstruction of labor</u> is suspected.

* Perform <u>intrapartum</u> transabdominal <u>ultrasound</u> to determine <u>fetal presentation</u>; , if possible.

* Initiate <u>cardiotocography</u>.

* Perform <u>emergency preoperative evaluation</u>.

* Pursue definitive <u>fetal presentation</u>-based management.





> [!TIP]
> Transabdominal <u>ultrasound</u> is more accurate than digital cervical examination for determining fetal head position. [[17]](/library/tp1Xr30)




#### <u>Fetal presentation</u>-based management




* <u>Compound presentation</u> [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[18]](/library/-HWDG50)

* Most patients: <u>expectant management</u>

* <u>Arrested labor</u> or <u>umbilical cord prolapse</u>: <u>cesarean delivery</u>

* Persistent <u>occiput posterior position</u> [[19]](/library/ZsWZt50)

* Most patients: <u>expectant management</u> or consider manual rotation to the occipital <u>anterior</u> position

* <u>Arrested labor</u>: <u>cesarean delivery</u>

* <u>Shoulder dystocia</u>: See “<u>Shoulder dystocia</u>.”

* <u>Transverse lie</u>: : <u>cesarean delivery</u>

* <u>Breech presentation</u> [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[20]](/library/3wYSir)

* Proceed with emergency vaginal delivery if <u>birth</u> appears imminent.

* Allow delivery up to the <u>umbilicus</u> using maternal effort.

* If the legs do not deliver, flex the fetal knees and sweep the legs out.

* Allow delivery up to the <u>scapula</u> using maternal effort.

* If the arms do not deliver, rotate the fetus to deliver the shoulder under the <u>pubic symphysis</u>, then rotate the fetus to deliver the other shoulder.

* Perform the <u>Mauriceau maneuver</u> to deliver the head.





### Complications [[8]](/library/8HWOH50)[[21]](/library/FgcgCb0)




#### Fetal




* <u>Birth asphyxia</u>

* Infection (intrauterine and neonatal)

* <u>Intracranial hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Birth injuries</u>

* <u>Perinatal</u> <u>death</u>





#### Maternal




* <u>Vesicovaginal fistula</u> and <u>ureterovaginal fistula</u>

* <u>Uterine rupture</u>

* Infection (e.g., <u>postpartum sepsis</u>)

* <u>Postpartum hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Stress urinary incontinence</u>

## Shoulder dystocia

### Definition [[22]](/library/f6Wk4m0)



* An obstetric emergency in which the <u>anterior</u> shoulder of the fetus becomes impacted behind the maternal <u>pubic symphysis</u> during vaginal delivery, or, less commonly, the <u>posterior</u> shoulder becomes impacted against the sacral promontory




### <u>Epidemiology</u>



* ∼ 0.2–3% of vaginal deliveries with <u>vertex presentation</u> [[22]](/library/f6Wk4m0)




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[22]](/library/f6Wk4m0)




* History of <u>shoulder dystocia</u>

* Fetal <u>macrosomia</u>

* <u>Maternal diabetes</u> mellitus or <u>gestational diabetes</u>

* Maternal <u>obesity</u>

* <u>Prolonged second stage of labor</u>





> [!TIP]
> Always be prepared for <u>shoulder dystocia</u>, as it can occur even in the absence of <u>risk factors</u>. [[22]](/library/f6Wk4m0)




### Clinical features




* Inability to deliver either shoulder with gentle downward <u>traction</u> on the fetal head

* Turtle sign: <u>retraction</u> of the partially delivered fetal head against the <u>perineum</u>

* Failed restitution of the fetal head





![Shoulder dystocia](media/npq6ali0ahcmqmfx0yft02aq.jpg)

Shoulder dystocia




### Management




For general management of vaginal delivery, see “<u>Manually assisted vaginal delivery</u>.”




#### Approach [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[22]](/library/f6Wk4m0)[[23]](/library/sGWt0M0)




* Establish the presence of <u>shoulder dystocia</u> (<u>clinical diagnosis</u>).

* Declare the presence of <u>shoulder dystocia</u>.

* Call for obstetrics, neonatology, anesthesia, and additional nursing staff.

* Inform the mother and instruct them not to push.

* Consider <u>insertion of a Foley catheter</u> to decompress the <u>bladder</u>.

* Perform initial <u>shoulder dystocia maneuvers</u>, starting with the <u>McRoberts maneuver</u>.  [[23]](/library/sGWt0M0)

* Proceed to secondary <u>shoulder dystocia maneuvers</u> if initial maneuvers are unsuccessful.

* If the <u>infant</u> has still not been delivered, consider maneuvers of last resort (e.g., intentional <u>clavicular fracture</u>).





#### Shoulder dystocia maneuvers [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[20]](/library/3wYSir)[[24]](/library/g6WF4m0)




* Initial maneuvers

* McRoberts maneuver  

* The patient should stop bearing down and lie <u>supine</u> with the buttocks on the edge of the bed.

* <u>Abduct</u>, externally rotate, and hyperflex the maternal hips (with the maternal legs pulled towards the head).

* <u>McRoberts maneuver</u> with suprapubic pressure (Rubin I maneuver)   [[22]](/library/f6Wk4m0)

* Manual delivery of the <u>posterior</u> fetal arm

* Secondary maneuvers

* Rubin II maneuver: Manually rotate the fetal <u>shoulder girdle</u> by applying pressure to the <u>posterior</u> part of the <u>anterior</u> shoulder.

* Woods corkscrew maneuver: Manually rotate the fetal <u>shoulder girdle</u> by applying pressure to the <u>anterior</u> part of the <u>posterior</u> shoulder.

* Gaskin maneuver (all fours positions)

* The patient moves into hands and knees position.

* Rubin and Woods maneuvers can be repeated.

* Maneuvers of last resort

* Intentional <u>clavicular fracture</u>: <u>Fracture</u> the <u>clavicle</u> by pulling the midportion of the <u>clavicle</u> upward or outward.

* Zavanelli maneuver: The fetal head is pushed back into the <u>pelvis</u> to alleviate pressure on the <u>umbilical cord</u> while the patient is transported to the OR for <u>cesarean delivery</u>.

* Symphysiotomy: surgical separation of the <u>anterior</u> fibers of the symphyseal <u>ligament</u>, only performed if all other maneuvers are unsuccessful and <u>cesarean delivery</u> is not available





> [!TIP]
> Internal maneuvers (i.e., maneuvers requiring direct manipulation of fetal parts) may require <u>episiotomy</u> and can be performed together with the <u>McRoberts maneuver</u>. [[24]](/library/g6WF4m0)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid excessive downward or <u>lateral</u> <u>traction</u> on the fetal head and neck, as this can result in <u>brachial plexus injuries</u>. [[23]](/library/sGWt0M0)




![McRoberts maneuver](media/small_61894712bbdfe.jpg)

McRoberts maneuver

![McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure (Rubin I maneuver) in shoulder dystocia](media/o8vgzifslwy7udyxylh65pcn.jpg)

McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure (Rubin I maneuver) in shoulder dystocia

![Rubin's maneuver](media/small_618946a3dc71b.jpg)

Rubin's maneuver




### Complications [[23]](/library/sGWt0M0)




* Fetal

* <u>Brachial plexus injury</u> (<u>Erb palsy</u> is more common than <u>Klumpke palsy</u>) [[25]](/library/ho1cb30)

* <u>Clavicle</u> or <u>humerus fracture</u>

* <u>Perinatal asphyxia and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy</u>

* Maternal

* <u>Perineal lacerations</u>

* <u>Postpartum hemorrhage</u>

## Abnormal rupture of membranes

### Definitions [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)




* Prelabor rupture of membranes (<u>PROM</u>): <u>rupture of membranes</u> before the onset of <u>labor</u> at ≥ 37 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (<u>PPROM</u>): <u>rupture of membranes</u> before the onset of <u>labor</u> and before 37 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Prolonged rupture of membranes: <u>rupture of membranes</u> > 18 hours before the onset of <u>labor</u> [[27]](/library/UtWb1M0)





### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)




The following values pertain to patients in the US:




* <u>PROM</u>: ∼ 8% of <u>pregnancies</u>

* <u>PPROM</u>: ∼ 2–3% of <u>pregnancies</u>





### <u>Risk factors</u> for <u>PPROM</u> [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)[[28]](/library/ftWk1M0)




<u>Risk factors</u> for <u>PPROM</u> are similar to <u>risk factors for preterm labor</u>, e.g.:




* History of <u>PPROM</u>

* <u>Short cervical length</u>

* <u>Antepartum bleeding</u>

* History of <u>sexually transmitted infections</u>

* Prior prenatal procedures (e.g., <u>cervical cerclage</u>, <u>amniocentesis</u>)

* Low <u>BMI</u>

* Low <u>socioeconomic status</u>

* <u>Cigarette smoking</u>

* <u>Substance use disorder</u>





### Diagnostics for abnormal rupture of membranes [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>: a sudden gush of pale yellow or clear fluid from the <u>vagina</u>

* Sterile <u>speculum examination</u>

* Fluid exiting the <u>cervix</u> and pooling in the <u>vaginal fornix</u> suggests <u>rupture of membranes</u>.

* Detection of amniotic fluid

* Litmus test or nitrazine test: Test strips turn blue, as <u>amniotic fluid</u> is alkaline.

* Positive fern test: fern pattern on glass slide

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: <u>Oligohydramnios</u> may be present.





> [!WARNING]
> Do not perform a digital cervical examination unless the patient is in active <u>labor</u> because it increases the risk of infection and has minimal diagnostic utility. [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)




### Management [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)[[28]](/library/ftWk1M0)




#### Initial management




* Consult <u>OB/GYN</u> to determine appropriate management.

* Determine <u>gestational age</u> and <u>fetal presentation</u>, and perform a <u>fetal status assessment</u>.

* Establish if <u>intrapartum prophylactic antibiotics for GBS</u> are required.

* Evaluate for indications for urgent delivery, e.g.:

* <u>Fetal distress</u>

* Intrauterine infection (e.g., <u>chorioamnionitis</u>)

* <u>Placental abruption</u>

* If necessary, initiate transfer to a hospital that can provide maternal and neonatal care.





#### Management by <u>gestational age</u>




* ≥ 37 0/7 weeks' <u>gestation</u> [[29]](/library/4D13eQ0)

* Initiate <u>induction of labor</u> with <u>manually assisted vaginal delivery</u>.

* Consider <u>expectant management</u> for up to 12–24 hours for patients with reassuring maternal and fetal status and without <u>GBS</u> infection.   [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)

* 34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Consider <u>expectant management</u> or <u>induction of labor</u> on a case-by-case basis.  [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)

* Consider <u>steroids</u> for <u>induction of fetal lung maturity</u>.

* 24 0/7 to 33 6/7 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Initiate <u>expectant management</u>.

* Administer <u>steroids</u> for <u>induction of fetal lung maturity</u>.

* Administer <u>PPROM antibiotic prophylaxis</u>.

* Consider up to 48 hours of <u>tocolysis</u> to inhibit uterine contractions in consultation with <u>OB/GYN</u>.

* Consider <u>magnesium sulfate</u> for <u>fetal neuroprotection</u> if delivery at < 32 weeks' <u>gestation</u> is anticipated. [[30]](/library/LAWw4L0)

* < 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Discuss the risks and benefits of <u>expectant management</u> vs. terminating the <u>pregnancy</u>, including predicted neonatal outcomes.

* Consider <u>maternal-fetal medicine</u> and neonatology consultation for patients who choose <u>expectant management</u>.

* Consider <u>PPROM antibiotic prophylaxis</u>.

* <u>GBS prophylaxis</u>, <u>corticosteroids</u>, <u>tocolysis</u>, and <u>magnesium sulfate</u> are not recommended before 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>.





#### PPROM antibiotic prophylaxis




* Goals

* Prolong <u>pregnancy</u> (reduce the risk of <u>gestational age</u>-dependent <u>morbidity</u>)

* Reduce the risk of maternal and <u>neonatal infections</u>

* Indication: <u>PPROM</u> at 20 0/7 to 33 6/7 weeks' <u>gestation</u> [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)

* Treatment

* Initial 48 hours: <u>ampicillin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE PLUS <u>erythromycin</u> IV (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)

* Subsequent 5 days: <u>amoxicillin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE PLUS <u>erythromycin</u> PO (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)

* Alternative: A single dose of <u>azithromycin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE may replace the 7-day course of <u>erythromycin</u>.





### Complications [[26]](/library/R8Xlm-)[[28]](/library/ftWk1M0)




* <u>PROM</u>: intrauterine infection (risk increases with duration of ruptured membranes)

* <u>PPROM</u>

* Fetal

* <u>Complications of prematurity</u> (e.g., neonatal <u>respiratory distress</u>, <u>necrotizing enterocolitis</u>)

* <u>Umbilical cord compression</u>

* Antepartum <u>death</u>

* Maternal

* <u>Chorioamnionitis</u>

* <u>Placental abruption</u>

---

## Umbilical cord complications

### Umbilical cord presentation [[31]](/library/dpWoom0)




* Definition: the presentation of the <u>umbilical cord</u> at the internal <u>cervical os</u> before the <u>fetal presenting part</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: <u>incidence</u> ∼ 0.6% [[31]](/library/dpWoom0)

* Clinical features: typically absent; soft pulsatile mass may be palpable on <u>pelvic examination</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>obstetric ultrasound</u>

* Management

* Before <u>labor</u>: close <u>obstetrician</u> follow-up with <u>labor</u> and delivery planning (e.g., attempted vaginal delivery, scheduled <u>cesarean delivery</u>)

* During <u>labor</u>: Prepare for <u>umbilical cord prolapse</u>.





![Cord presentation](media/hetb1mgdcz718q1a2lmcv1v8.jpg)

Cord presentation




### Umbilical cord prolapse [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[31]](/library/dpWoom0)




#### Definitions




* Overt umbilical cord prolapse: the descent of the <u>umbilical cord</u> into the cervical canal or <u>vagina</u> before the <u>fetal presenting part</u> after <u>rupture of membranes</u>

* Occult umbilical cord prolapse: the descent of the <u>umbilical cord</u> into the cervical canal or <u>vagina</u> alongside the <u>fetal presenting part</u> after <u>rupture of membranes</u>





![Overt umbilical cord prolapse](media/mdysg5u82s3o66oyrtnwv9ek.jpg)

Overt umbilical cord prolapse




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>Incidence</u> 0.1–0.4% [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Estimated <u>perinatal</u> mortality ∼ 10% [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





#### Etiology




* <u>Spontaneous rupture of membranes</u>

* <u>Iatrogenic</u> (e.g., <u>artificial rupture of membranes</u>, insertion of transcervical balloon catheters)

* <u>Risk factors</u> include:

* Fetal <u>risk factors</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Malpresentation</u> (e.g., <u>breech presentation</u>, <u>transverse lie</u>)

* <u>Prematurity</u>

* Fetal weight < 2500 g

* Long <u>umbilical cord</u>

* Maternal <u>risk factors</u>, e.g.:

* Grand <u>multiparity</u>

* Uterine abnormalities





#### Diagnostics




* <u>Pelvic examination</u>: : visible or palpable <u>umbilical cord</u>

* <u>Fetal heart rate</u>: : prolonged fetal <u>bradycardia</u> or repetitive moderate to severe <u>variable decelerations</u>





#### Management




* Immediately consult obstetrics, anesthesia, and neonatology to prepare for emergency delivery.

* Initiate <u>cardiotocography</u> to monitor <u>fetal heart rate</u> and the <u>effectiveness</u> of interventions.

* Relieve <u>umbilical cord compression</u> and maintain interventions until delivery, i.e.:

* Manually elevate the <u>fetal presenting part</u>.

* Position the patient in the <u>Trendelenburg position</u> and/or <u>knee-chest position</u>.

* Consider filling the <u>bladder</u> with 500–750 mL of saline.  [[32]](/library/UBWbZL0)

* Consider manual reduction of the prolapsed cord and rapid vaginal delivery if immediate <u>cesarean delivery</u> is not possible.





> [!WARNING]
> Minimize manipulation of the prolapsed cord, as this can cause vasospasm and fetal <u>hypoxia</u>.




### Nuchal cord [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[33]](/library/bsWHt50)




* Definition: the wrapping of the <u>umbilical cord</u> 360 degrees around the fetal neck

* Etiology: most often caused by fetal movement

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[34]](/library/jGW__50)

* Single cord loop around the neck: ∼ 16% of births

* Multiple cord loops around the neck: ∼ 4% of births

* Diagnosis

* Before <u>labor</u>: may be seen on <u>ultrasound</u>

* During <u>labor</u>: <u>clinical diagnosis</u>

* Management 

* Before <u>labor</u>: close <u>obstetrician</u> follow-up with <u>labor</u> and delivery planning (e.g., attempted vaginal delivery, scheduled <u>cesarean delivery</u>)

* During <u>labor</u>

* Reduce by slipping loose nuchal cords over the head at the maternal <u>perineum</u>.

* If unable to reduce, double clamp and cut the cord, then proceed with rapid <u>manually assisted vaginal delivery</u>.





![Manually assisted vaginal delivery](media/p428ouy7jxp5buak5acp2cgq.jpg)

Manually assisted vaginal delivery




### Knotting of the umbilical cord




* Etiology: most often caused by fetal movement

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: ∼ 1% of births [[35]](/library/SGWyA50)

* Management

* Before <u>labor</u>: close <u>obstetrician</u> follow-up with <u>labor</u> and delivery planning (e.g., attempted vaginal delivery, scheduled <u>cesarean delivery</u>) [[36]](/library/QpWu6m0)

* During <u>labor</u>: Proceed with <u>manually assisted vaginal delivery</u>; avoid <u>cord traction</u>.  [[16]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





![True umbilical cord knot](media/my9lptpevv2du2zqplk5hw8j.jpg)

True umbilical cord knot

![False umbilical cord knot](media/amrh0l5idtgr0pkxnrcx25g2.jpg)

False umbilical cord knot

## Induction of labor

### Indications for induction of labor




* <u>Post-term</u> <u>pregnancy</u> (≥ 42 weeks of <u>pregnancy</u> or <u>gestation</u>)

* <u>PPROM</u> after 34 weeks

* <u>PROM</u> at term

* <u>Hypertension</u> during <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>preeclampsia</u>, <u>eclampsia</u>, <u>HELLP syndrome</u>

* <u>Maternal diabetes</u> to avoid <u>post-term</u> <u>pregnancy</u> (risk of <u>macrosomia</u>)

* Maternal request at term

* <u>Intrauterine fetal demise</u>





### Contraindications for induction of labor [[37]](/library/raWfNP0)




* History of <u>uterine rupture</u>; previous <u>classical cesarean incision</u>

* Complete <u>placenta previa</u>

* <u>Vasa previa</u>

* <u>Transverse fetal lie</u>

* Cord prolapse

* Active maternal <u>genital herpes</u>

* <u>Nonreassuring fetal heart rate</u>





### Bishop score [[37]](/library/raWfNP0)




#### Overview




* Definition: a scoring system used to assess the <u>cervix</u> and the likelihood of successful <u>induction of labor</u>

* Interpretation 

* <u>Bishop score</u> ≥ 8: favorable <u>cervix</u> (ready for vaginal delivery)

* <u>Bishop score</u> ≤ 6: unfavorable <u>cervix</u> (not ready for vaginal delivery)

* Alternative: simplified Bishop score [[38]](/library/nGW7-50)

* Considers only <u>fetal station</u>, <u>cervical dilation</u>, and <u>cervical effacement</u>

* A score of ≥ 5 indicates a favorable <u>cervix</u>.





#### <u>Bishop score</u>




| <br><u>Bishop score</u> [[37]](/library/raWfNP0)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Score |  |  |  |
| 0 points | 1 point | 2 points | 3 points |  |
| Cervical position | <u>Posterior</u> | Midline | <u>Anterior</u> |  |
| Cervical consistency | Firm | Moderately firm | Soft (ripe) |  |
| <u>Cervical effacement</u> | ≤ 30% | 31–50% | 51–80% | > 80% |
| <u>Cervical dilation</u> | Closed | 1–2 cm | 3–4 cm | ≥ 5 cm |
| <u>Fetal station</u> | -3 cm | -2 cm | -1/0 cm | +1/+2 cm |





### Approach




* <u>Membrane sweeping</u> (shortens time to onset of <u>labor</u>)

* If the <u>cervix</u> is still unfavorable: <u>cervical ripening</u> with <u>prostaglandin E1</u> or E2 (e.g., <u>misoprostol</u>)

* Maternal <u>oxytocin</u> infusion

* Consider <u>amniotomy</u> (only if the <u>cervix</u> is partially dilated and completely effaced, and the fetal head is well applied)

* Administer under <u>fetal heart rate</u> monitoring.





### Failure of induction [[5]](/library/CAdqNs0)




* Definition: a prolonged latent phase (e.g., 12–18 hours) after <u>induction of labor</u> (i.e., initiation of <u>oxytocin</u> and <u>rupture of membranes</u>) [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)[[5]](/library/CAdqNs0)[[39]](/library/Lzdwts0)

* Management

* Maternal and/or <u>fetal distress</u>: <u>intrauterine resuscitation</u> and/or immediate delivery

* Reassuring maternal and fetal signs: <u>cesarean delivery</u> after 18 hours of failed induction  [[1]](/library/cRdaNp0)

---

## Assisted vaginal delivery

### Obstetric forceps delivery [[40]](/library/CCaq85)




* Definition: a forcep is a metal device that enables gentle rotation and/or <u>traction</u> of the fetal head during vaginal delivery

* Types 

* Kielland: enables rotation and <u>traction</u> of the fetal head

* Simpson: only enables <u>traction</u> of the fetal head

* Barton: used for <u>occiput transverse position</u> of the fetal head

* Piper: used to deliver the fetal head during <u>breech delivery</u>

* Classification (See “Station” in “<u>Mechanics of childbirth</u>”)

* Outlet: fetal head lies on the <u>pelvic floor</u>

* Low: fetal head is below +2 station (not on the <u>pelvic floor</u>)

* Mid: fetal head is below 0 station (not at +2 station)

* High: fetal head is not engaged

* Indications

* <u>Prolonged second stage of labor</u>

* <u>Breech presentation</u>

* <u>Nonreassuring fetal heart rate</u>

* To avoid/assist maternal pushing efforts (e.g., maternal fatigue or cardiopulmonary conditions)

* Prerequisites

* Skilled clinician

* Clinically adequate <u>pelvic</u> dimensions (see “<u>Mechanics of childbirth</u>”)

* Full <u>cervical dilation</u>

* Engagement of the fetal head

* Knowledge of exact position and attitude of the fetal head

* Emptied maternal <u>bladder</u>

* No suspicion of fetal bleeding or bone mineralization disorders

* Advantages (compared to <u>vacuum delivery</u>)

* Scalp injuries are less common

* Cannot undergo decompression and “pop off”

* Complications

* Maternal: <u>obstetric lacerations</u> (<u>cervix</u>, <u>vagina</u>, <u>uterus</u>), perineal <u>hematomas</u>, <u>urinary tract</u> injury, anal sphincter injury

* Fetal: head or <u>soft tissue</u> trauma (e.g., <u>scalp lacerations</u>, injured <u>ears</u>), <u>facial nerve palsy</u>, <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u>, <u>retinal hemorrhage</u>, <u>skull fractures</u>, fetal <u>death</u> (rare)





![Types of obstetric forceps](media/cumihgak369cr13q9ff0f0oz.jpg)

Types of obstetric forceps

![Forceps delivery](media/i30o9el0bvk4ta0cu1peardq.jpg)

Forceps delivery




### Vacuum extractor delivery [[40]](/library/CCaq85)




* Definition: a vacuum extractor is a metal or plastic cup, attached to the fetal head with a suction device, that enables <u>traction</u> of the fetal head during vaginal delivery

* Indications

* <u>Prolonged second stage of labor</u>

* <u>Nonreassuring fetal heart rate</u>

* To avoid/assist maternal pushing efforts

* Prerequisites

* Skilled clinician

* Clinically adequate <u>pelvic</u> dimensions

* <u>Gestation</u> ≥ 34 weeks

* Engagement of the fetal head

* Full <u>cervical dilation</u>

* Emptied maternal <u>bladder</u>

* Vertex position

* No suspicion of fetal bleeding or bone mineralization disorders

* Advantages (compared to <u>forceps delivery</u>)

* Requires minimum space

* ↓ <u>incidence</u> of third- and fourth-degree <u>perineal tears</u>

* Less knowledge about exact position and attitude of the fetal head is acceptable

* Complications

* Maternal: suction of maternal <u>soft tissue</u> → <u>hematomas</u> or <u>lacerations</u>

* Fetal: <u>cephalohematoma</u>  , <u>scalp lacerations</u>, life-threatening <u>head injury</u> (e.g., <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u> or <u>subgaleal hematoma</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> A routine <u>episiotomy</u> is not recommended with <u>assisted vaginal delivery</u> because of the risk of poor healing and anal sphincter injury!




> [!TIP]
> An advantage of <u>assisted vaginal delivery</u> is avoiding <u>cesarean delivery</u>.




![Vacuum extractor](media/ilht1g8g5fbklmppuz7vqzyb.jpg)

Vacuum extractor

![Vacuum extractor delivery](media/xwtqegigop96ybdoxsunc8hg.jpg)

Vacuum extractor delivery

![Scalp after vacuum extractor delivery](media/whf2iox5b2nrijjwp18ybhd0.jpg)

Scalp after vacuum extractor delivery

## Intrauterine resuscitation

<u>Intrauterine resuscitation</u> focuses on improving <u>oxygen delivery</u> to the <u>placenta</u> and maintaining umbilical blood flow to treat <u>fetal distress</u> and enable safe delivery.




* Indication: <u>nonreassuring fetal status</u>

* Initial management

* Consult obstetrics immediately.

* <u>Reposition</u> the mother from <u>supine</u> to the <u>lateral decubitus position</u>.

* Administer a 1L IV fluid bolus. [[41]](/library/XGW9B50)

* Provide <u>oxygen therapy</u> if there is maternal <u>hypoxia</u>.  [[42]](/library/JtWseM0)[[43]](/library/n8W7MM0)

* Discontinue <u>uterotonic agents</u> (e.g., <u>oxytocin</u>, <u>misoprostol</u>).

* Consider modifying maternal pushing efforts (e.g., temporary cessation, pushing with alternate contractions).

* Obstetric management; consider the following:

* <u>Tocolysis</u> (e.g., for uterine tachysystole: > 5 contractions within 10 minutes)

* <u>Amnioinfusion</u> [[44]](/library/3AWSjL0)

* Emergency <u>cesarean delivery</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Use <u>IV fluids</u> with caution in patients with <u>cardiomyopathy</u> or <u>preeclampsia</u>, as these patients have an increased risk of <u>hypervolemia</u>, which can lead to <u>pulmonary edema</u>. [[45]](/library/jpW_6m0)
